slides.title: Room 5: Faith and Church
slides.narration: Welcome to Lesson 10. This room is about faith and church, and it is where two people can use the same word and imagine very different lives.

slides.quote: “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly, teaching and admonishing one another in all wisdom, singing psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, with thankfulness in your hearts to God. And whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.”
slides.narration:
Let’s begin with Scripture. Colossians chapter 3, verses 16 and 17.

“Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly, teaching and admonishing one another in all wisdom, singing psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, with thankfulness in your hearts to God. And whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.”

slides.kicker: Notice who Paul is writing to
slides.title: A letter to a church
body: This is not a marriage manual. These verses describe the shape of Christian life together, and we draw from them for the home.
slides.narration: First, notice who Paul is writing to. This is a letter to a church, not a manual for marriages. The teaching on marriage comes a little later in the same chapter. So these two verses describe the shape of Christian life together, and we draw from them for the home.

slides.title: Let the word of Christ dwell richly
body: Not visit. Not appear on Sundays. It is meant to be at home among believers, shaping how they teach, correct, encourage, sing and give thanks.
slides.narration: Notice what he asks. “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly.” Not visit. Not appear on Sundays. Dwell, and richly. The word of Christ is meant to be at home among believers, shaping how they teach, correct and encourage one another, and how they sing and give thanks.

slides.title: “Whatever you do, in word or deed”
body: Faith is not one compartment of life. It covers ordinary words and ordinary deeds, done with thankfulness.
slides.narration: And notice the second sentence. “Whatever you do, in word or deed, do everything in the name of the Lord Jesus.” Faith is not one compartment of life. It covers the whole of it, ordinary words and ordinary deeds, done with thankfulness.

slides.title: An ordinary Tuesday as much as a Sunday
body: A Christian home is not one with many church activities. It is one where Christ’s word shapes how you worship, decide, speak and love.
slides.narration: That is the truth this lesson stands on. A Christian home is not one that holds a great many church activities. It is one where Christ’s word shapes how you worship, decide, speak and love, on an ordinary Tuesday as much as on a Sunday.

slides.title: Not supervisor and pupil
body: Paul describes believers ministering the word to one another. It warns against treating one spouse as the permanent spiritual supervisor.
slides.narration: And notice the phrase “teaching and admonishing one another.” Paul describes believers ministering the word to one another. Applied to marriage, this warns us against treating one spouse as the permanent spiritual supervisor and the other as merely the pupil.

body: Not “Do we both believe in Jesus?” but: can we build a marriage in which our faith draws us toward God, truth and each other, even when our journeys are not identical?
slides.narration: So there is a question for each of you before you marry, and it is not “Do we both believe in Jesus?” It is: can we build a marriage in which our faith draws us toward God, toward truth, and toward each other, even when our spiritual journeys are not identical?

slides.kicker: Here is how it goes wrong
slides.title: Two pictures of “Christian”
body: “Deeply involved, at church several times a week.” “We’ll attend, pray, live as Christians, but family life won’t revolve around church programmes.”
slides.sub: Either may be faithful, if you understand what it requires and freely agree.
slides.narration:
Here is how it usually goes wrong.

Two people agree on the word “Christian” without ever defining what it means in the daily running of a marriage. One imagines: “We’ll be deeply involved. Serving, evangelising, at church several times a week, our children raised right in the middle of it.” The other, just as sincerely: “We’ll attend, we’ll pray, we’ll live as Christians, but our family life won’t revolve around church programmes.”

Either pattern may be faithful, but only if the couple understands what it will require and freely agrees to it. Both people mean it. Neither has said it out loud.

slides.title: Each quietly disappointed
body: One feels their spouse is spiritually passive. The other feels the marriage is consumed by commitments never agreed to.
slides.narration: Then they are married, and within a year one feels their spouse is spiritually passive, and the other feels their marriage is being consumed by commitments they never agreed to. Each is quietly disappointed, and neither can say why, because on paper they agreed about everything.

slides.title: To “what does our faith require?”
body: What role has prayer? What does church mean to each of us? How much time for ministry before it costs the marriage?
slides.narration: So the conversation has to move from “are we Christians?” to “what does our faith actually require of the marriage we are building?” Ask questions that bring faith out of the abstract and into ordinary weeks. What role does prayer have? Do I expect us to pray together daily? What does going to church mean to each of us? How much time am I willing to give to ministry before it starts costing the marriage?

slides.kicker: A phrase that does no work until explained
slides.title: “Spiritual leadership”
body: Two people can use it and picture entirely different arrangements. Say what you mean, concretely.
slides.narration: And here is a phrase that does almost no work until you explain it: “spiritual leadership.” Two people can both use it and picture entirely different arrangements. One imagines someone who decides. Another imagines someone who serves. Another imagines someone who leads devotions on Sunday evenings and otherwise decides jointly. So say what you mean, concretely.

slides.title: Faith when nobody can see it
body: What would my faith look like if nobody at church could see it? That separates a spiritual life from church activity.
slides.narration: Now, one question is worth sitting with: what would my faith look like if nobody at church could see it? That separates a spiritual life from church activity. They overlap in healthy people, and can be quite distinct in others, and you should each know which you are marrying.

slides.title: What does your faith look like on an ordinary Tuesday, when nobody from church can see it?
body: Take a moment before you go on.
slides.narration: Pause here. What does your faith look like on an ordinary Tuesday, when nobody from church can see it? Take a moment before you go on.

slides.title: Both Christians, at different places
body: One prays, reads and serves. The other believes sincerely and rarely does those things with discipline.
slides.sub: Not automatic grounds for calling off a wedding. Can you respect each other’s actual reality and build on it?
slides.narration:
Now the most sensitive part. Sometimes both people are genuinely Christians and simply at different places. One prays regularly, reads Scripture, serves, thinks about faith constantly. The other believes in Christ sincerely and rarely does any of those things with much discipline.

That is not automatic grounds for calling off a wedding. But it does matter, and it will not stay quiet. The real question is: can the two of you respect each other’s actual current reality, and build a marriage on that?

slides.title: Marrying a future version
body: “Once we’re married, I’ll bring them along.” “I’ll agree rather than risk losing the relationship.”
slides.narration: Two dangerous assumptions turn up here, usually one in each person. The partner who wants more church involvement may think, “Once we’re married, I’ll bring them along.” The partner who wants less may think, “I don’t want this level of activity, but I’ll agree rather than risk losing the relationship.” Both are marrying a future version of the other person, and neither has said so. This is the people-pleasing from Lesson 1, and the hoping-marriage-will-change-it from Lesson 3, appearing together in the most spiritually loaded room in the house.

body: If your partner’s present practices stayed the same, could you still freely choose this marriage? Or are you agreeing to a life you do not want?
slides.narration: So each of you answers your own question. To the one who wants more shared spiritual activity: if your partner’s present practices stayed the same, could you still freely choose this marriage? And to the other: if your partner’s level of commitment stays exactly where it is, can you live peacefully with that for the long term, or are you agreeing to a life you do not want?

slides.title: Discuss what touches the marriage
body: Which church, how you will worship, how children are raised in the faith. Baptism, the Lord’s Supper and spiritual authority in the home deserve a proper conversation.
slides.narration: Different denominations can be manageable, but only if you discuss what actually touches the marriage: which church, how you will worship, how you hope to raise any children in the faith, and what you will do when your traditions teach different things. A difference in style is usually negotiable. A genuine disagreement about baptism, the Lord’s Supper, spiritual authority in the home, or how children come into the faith is a different order of thing, and deserves a proper conversation rather than a hopeful one.

slides.title: Not length of church involvement
body: Maturity shows in humility, faithfulness, self-control, repentance, love, truthfulness, and willingness to be corrected.
slides.narration:
And now the hardest part of this room. Do not let “more spiritually mature” become a synonym for “more spiritually important.” Long church involvement does not by itself demonstrate spiritual maturity. Maturity shows in character: humility, faithfulness, self-control, repentance, love, truthfulness, and the willingness to be corrected.

Neither person should use this room to instruct the other to become a copy of themselves. Ask a harder question instead: what kind of Christian spouse am I actually becoming?

slides.title: Do not marry someone’s spiritual potential
body: Marry the person in front of you. A marriage should not be a private project to fix, convert, disciple or upgrade your spouse.
slides.narration: And one instruction above all: do not marry someone’s spiritual potential. Marry the person in front of you. People grow enormously after marriage, and we should hope and pray they do. But a marriage should not be founded on a private project to fix, convert, disciple or upgrade your spouse. That makes one of you a perpetual disappointment and the other a perpetual supervisor.

slides.title: Say it now
body: If either of you is in a period of real doubt, say so before carrying it silently into a marriage where the other believes they are marrying certainty.
slides.narration: If either of you is in a period of real doubt, that is worth saying now. It is far better said now than carried silently into a marriage where the other person believes they are marrying certainty.

slides.title: About twenty minutes
list: What does my faith look like on an ordinary Tuesday?
slides.sub: You do not have to write anything down.
slides.narration: Your step has two parts. First, about twenty minutes alone with the questions in the worksheet. Where am I actually, spiritually, not where I would like to be? What does my faith look like on an ordinary Tuesday? Where do I struggle? What do I doubt? Many Christians carry questions or doubts they have found difficult to express. You do not have to write anything down.

slides.title: 45 to 60 minutes
list: Where are we each spiritually, and what does an ordinary week look like?
What would a realistic week of worship, service, prayer, rest and time together look like?
Am I hoping you will become something different?
slides.note: You control the details and pace of what you share. But if your beliefs or doubts materially affect the marriage your partner believes you are building, speak honestly.
slides.narration: Then set aside 45 to 60 minutes, together, when neither of you is tired. Have your Lesson 2 rules in front of you. Work through three main questions. First: where are we each spiritually, and what does our faith look like on an ordinary week? You control the details and pace of what you share. But if your present beliefs or doubts materially affect the Christian marriage your partner believes you are building, speak honestly about that before you marry. Second: what would a realistic week of worship, service, prayer, rest and time together look like for us? Third, and it is the honest one, out loud: am I hoping you will become something different from what you are now?

slides.kicker: If you find a real difference
slides.title: Record it
body: Do not smooth it over. Some convictions are non-negotiable: infant baptism, for instance, becomes concrete the moment there is a baby.
slides.sub: Continue the other questions over the coming weeks.
slides.narration:
If you find a real difference, do not smooth it over. Record it. Some convictions are non-negotiable, and infant baptism, for instance, becomes concrete the moment there is a baby. Identify those now, not in a maternity ward.

The other important questions, about giving, authority and decisions, and how your children will be raised in the faith, are worth continuing over the coming weeks. You do not need to settle them today.

body: Lord, thank You that Your word is meant to dwell among us. Help us build a home where faith is real, ordinary and honest. Keep us from using Your name to silence one another. Give us humility to receive one another as we are, and wisdom to grow together. Amen.
slides.narration:
Let me close with a short prayer.

Lord, thank You that Your word is meant to dwell among us. Help us build a home where faith is real, ordinary and honest. Keep us from using Your name to silence one another. Give us humility to receive one another as we are, and wisdom to grow together. Amen.
